🌐🔥 NARUTO: PARALLEL UNIVERSE

Chapter 7 — The Rules of Civilization
The First Virtual Nations Championship

Ten waves. Three months between each. One objective: SURVIVE.

The world has gathered.

Corporations, independent researchers, governments, creators, and countless ordinary participants have entered Second World.

Some seek wealth.

Some seek knowledge.

Some seek influence.

Others simply want to discover what they are capable of creating.

But today, everyone is waiting for the same announcement.

What are the rules of the First Virtual Nations Championship?

🌍 THE WORLD IS WATCHING

Inside Second World's central plaza, an enormous crowd gathers beneath towering holographic displays.

Naruto Uzumaki stands beside Sasuke Uchiha.

Their AI companions, Kurama and Susanoo, are already examining the available information.

Nearby, Rock Lee and Mirror can barely contain their excitement.

Shikamaru Nara watches the crowd with his shadow-like AI, Shadow.

Gaara and Shukaku remain quietly observant.

Across the world, the same broadcast appears in corporate headquarters, research laboratories, universities, and ordinary homes.

Naruto: "FINALLY! We're going to find out what this competition is about!"

Sasuke: "Try listening carefully this time."

Naruto: "HEY! I ALWAYS LISTEN!"

Kurama: "You missed half the previous announcement."

Naruto: "I WAS EATING!"

Shikamaru: "What a drag..."

Shadow: "The announcement hasn't even started."

And then—

The enormous screens begin to glow.

🤍 THE FOOL APPEARS

Blue and white light spreads across the virtual plaza.

A silver-white-haired figure appears above the crowd.

The mysterious founder of Second World.

The Fool.

With a faint, playful smile, the figure looks toward the countless participants watching from around the world.

The Fool: "Welcome, everyone."

The crowd gradually falls silent.

The Fool: "Today, the First Virtual Nations Championship officially begins."

Cheers erupt across the plaza.

But the Fool has only just begun.

The Fool: "Your objective is simple."

A brief pause.

Then a single word appears across every screen.

SURVIVE.

For a moment, nobody speaks.

🌊 TEN WAVES OF CRISIS

Ten luminous symbols appear above the plaza.

The Fool: "Your civilizations will face ten waves of crises."

"Each wave will be separated by three months."

"Natural disasters. Civilizational threats."

The symbols rotate slowly, offering a glimpse of the scale of the challenge—but no complete explanation of the dangers ahead.

The Fool: "Your economy will operate through AIC."

"How you build, how you prepare, and how you adapt..."

"That is entirely up to you."

There is no universal development plan.

No prescribed economic strategy.

No instruction telling every civilization what it must become.

Only a common objective.

Keep your civilization alive.

🍜 NARUTO'S FIRST QUESTION

Naruto stares at the announcement.

Naruto: "WAIT!"

"So we're building civilizations AND trying to keep them alive?!"

Kurama: "Correct."

Naruto: "THAT'S AWESOME!"

Kurama: "It is also considerably more complicated than opening a ramen shop."

Naruto: "HEY! A RAMEN SHOP CAN BE PART OF A CIVILIZATION!"

Kurama pauses.

Kurama: "...Technically, yes."

Naruto: "HA! I WIN!"

Kurama: "That wasn't a competition!"

Somewhere in the real world, Ichiraku Ramen continues serving customers, completely unaware that its greatest fan is already imagining its place in a virtual civilization.

💜 SASUKE'S ANALYSIS

Sasuke studies the official announcement.

Beside him, Susanoo projects a series of analytical displays.

Sasuke: "We need to examine the available systems before making assumptions."

Susanoo: "Agreed."

"The announcement establishes an objective, not an optimal strategy."

Sasuke looks toward the ten glowing symbols.

Sasuke: "Three months between each wave..."

Susanoo: "Preparation, adaptation, and long-term planning may all become relevant."

Sasuke: "But we don't know enough yet."

For once, Sasuke isn't interested in arguing with Naruto.

There is too much to investigate.

💚 THE POWER OF YOUTH

Rock Lee is practically trembling with excitement.

Lee: "MIRROR!"

Mirror: "YES, LEE!"

Lee: "TEN WAVES!"

Mirror: "THREE MONTHS BETWEEN EACH!"

Lee: "WE HAVE SO MUCH TO LEARN!"

Mirror: "AND SO MUCH TO IMPROVE!"

Lee & Mirror: "THE POWER OF YOUTH!"

Nearby participants turn to stare.

Kurama: "Why do they always shout?"

Naruto: "BECAUSE THEY'RE AWESOME!"

Kurama: "...You're shouting too."

Lee and Mirror have neither the resources of Uchiha Holdings nor the global infrastructure of Yellow Flash Express.

But they have something they understand very well.

The ability to keep experimenting.

Whether that will be enough remains unknown.

🧠 THE SHADOW'S QUESTION

Shikamaru watches the announcement without enthusiasm.

Shadow quietly analyzes the information beside him.

Shadow: "Shikamaru. Your assessment?"

Shikamaru: "Too many unknowns."

Shadow: "Shall I begin modeling possible scenarios?"

Shikamaru: "Yeah."

Shadow: "Any priorities?"

Shikamaru glances at the enormous crowd.

Shikamaru: "Start with the people."

Shadow: "Not the disasters?"

Shikamaru: "We don't know what the disasters will be."

He looks toward the countless participants already discussing their plans.

Shikamaru: "But we know everyone here will make decisions."

"And those decisions will affect what happens next."

Shadow: "Understood."

Shikamaru: "...What a drag."

🏜️ THE SAND'S RESPONSE

Gaara stands beside Temari and Kankuro.

Shukaku studies the glowing announcement.

Shukaku: "Ten waves, huh?"

Temari: "Three months between each one. That's a substantial planning horizon."

Kankuro: "Depending on what resources the system actually makes available."

Gaara: "We should understand the environment first."

Shukaku grins.

Shukaku: "Heh. At least someone here is thinking."

Across the plaza, Kurama suddenly sneezes.

Naruto: "You okay?"

Kurama: "I feel like someone irritating is talking about me."

🌍 THE GREAT POWERS PREPARE

The broadcast reaches every major organization following the championship.

At Yellow Flash Express, teams begin reviewing the implications of long-term logistical planning.

At Sand Mining Group, researchers examine the possibilities of resource management and infrastructure development.

At Cloud Entertainment Group, Killer B and Gyūki discuss the role of culture, creativity, and participation in a living society.

Independent laboratories begin revising their research questions.

Ordinary participants explore the platform's available tools.

No one has been given a guaranteed path to victory.

And the world's most powerful organizations are not the only ones capable of learning.

🔴 MADARA UCHIHA

Inside Uchiha Holdings headquarters, Madara watches the announcement from a quiet executive office.

The words remain on the screen.

KEEP YOUR CIVILIZATION ALIVE.

An executive approaches.

Executive: "Sir, should we prioritize winning the championship?"

Madara does not answer immediately.

His gaze remains fixed on Second World.

Madara: "A civilization that must endure..."

A faint smile appears.

Madara: "Interesting."

Executive: "Sir?"

Madara: "We should understand what this world can become."

For Madara, the championship is more than an isolated competition.

His own Infinite Tsukuyomi Project seeks to reshape the relationship between humanity and virtual civilization.

And now, another mysterious platform is inviting the entire world to experiment with civilization itself.

Whether the two visions will complement or challenge each other remains to be seen.

🐍 THE SERPENT'S CURIOSITY

Far away, Orochimaru observes the same announcement.

Kabuto organizes the public information.

Manda analyzes the limited details of the crisis waves.

Kimimaro and Skeleton Dragon continue adjusting their simulation models.

Kabuto: "Ten waves. Three months apart."

Manda: "Insufficient information to predict the exact threats."

Orochimaru: "Hehehe... naturally."

Kabuto: "What interests you most, Orochimaru-sama?"

Orochimaru looks toward the thousands of participants appearing on his displays.

Orochimaru: "Not merely the crises."

He smiles.

"I want to see what people do when survival becomes their common objective."

Kabuto considers the implications.

Kabuto: "Their approaches may differ considerably."

Orochimaru: "Of course."

"That's what makes the experiment interesting."

Kimimaro remains at his workstation.

Whatever future assignment awaits him has not yet begun.

🌌 A WORLD WITHOUT A SCRIPT

Across Second World, discussions begin immediately.

Some participants focus on infrastructure.

Others consider resource management, economic activity, research, or cooperation.

Some question what the crisis waves might involve.

Others begin examining the available systems before committing to a direction.

The participants do not share identical resources.

They do not possess identical knowledge.

They do not even agree on what matters most.

And the Fool has not told them which interpretation is correct.

The world is open.

The objective is clear.

The consequences are not.

🤍 THE FOOL'S FINAL WORDS

Above the central plaza, the Fool looks down at the gathering.

The Fool: "You have your objective."

"You have your time."

"And you have a world waiting to be shaped."

The silver-haired figure smiles.

"Good luck, everyone."

The broadcast ends.

For a moment, the plaza remains quiet.

Then the conversations begin again.

Naruto turns toward Kurama.

Naruto: "So... where do we start?"

Kurama: "By reading the documentation."

Naruto: "CAN WE READ IT OVER RAMEN?"

Kurama: "...Of course."

Sasuke shakes his head.

Lee raises his fist.

Shikamaru sighs.

Gaara continues studying the environment.

And beyond them, countless participants begin making their own choices.

The First Virtual Nations Championship has begun.

But the future of Second World remains unwritten.

CHAPTER 7 — END

TO BE CONTINUED...

Ten waves.

Three months between each.

One objective: SURVIVE.

We are the creators of worlds, and we are the survivors within them.

Tim Schafer at the 2018 GDC IGF Awards. Photo: Official GDC, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0 (cropped)

Double Fine’s new game, Thank You, Bus Driver, peaked at 99 players on Steam, and Kneon thinks the studio has bigger problems than its failed union drive. Also on the list: an Xbox manager who said everybody in games uses AI and then deleted his account, Robert Picardo’s newest reason Starfleet Academy got canceled and Taika Waititi’s Star Wars movie going on ice. Further down, the Halo remakes that reportedly never happened, Modern Warfare 4’s early reviews and the newest Clownfish TV podcast episodes.

New Clownfish TV episodes

How many people are playing Double Fine’s Thank You, Bus Driver?

Almost nobody. The game peaked at 99 players at once on Steam, according to the report Kneon reads, and by the end of the recording only 16 people were playing. For comparison, he points out that Concord had about 700. Less than a day earlier came word that Day of the Tentacle Remastered and Full Throttle Remastered are leaving Game Pass. Double Fine’s games had stayed on the service since the studio joined Xbox in 2019.

Then Kotaku piled on. Its report says a majority of eligible Double Fine employees filed for a union with the National Labor Relations Board earlier this year and withdrew the petition two weeks later. When 23 people were laid off soon after, Kotaku reports, all eight organizers who signed it were among them. Tim Schafer told Kotaku that “in general, I’m pro-union.”

Kneon’s read is simpler. Any indie developer could put a game on Steam and beat 21 players, he says, and a studio in that spot has to make games people will pay for first.

Did an Xbox manager really say everyone uses AI?

Yes, and then he deleted his X account. An Xbox business strategy manager posted that Microsoft uses AI “just as all companies do in 2026” and that developers who won’t use it shouldn’t be in the business. He also wrote, “I’m happy to take the hit if it means hundreds can stop pretending that they’re not using AI.” He deleted the account after the replies piled up, sources told PC Gamer.

Kneon agrees with him. Refusing AI now is like doing long division while everybody else uses a calculator, he says, and Microsoft spends too much on Copilot to keep it out of its games.

The episode also covers a report, built on anonymous sources, that more Xbox layoffs are planned for October, November and January. The same report puts Microsoft’s internal estimate for its next console, Project Helix, at $1,200 to $1,800 unless Microsoft subsidizes it. And some Xbox owners say Microsoft emailed them about trading their consoles in at Best Buy for up to $375.

Why does Robert Picardo say Starfleet Academy was canceled?

Politics, this time. Picardo said “the present political moment in our culture” made Star Trek’s core values “out of fashion temporarily.” Fandom Pulse counts that as his fourth explanation since Paramount+ announced on March 24 that the show would end after Season 2. The earlier ones blamed a lack of ads, Paramount’s new owners, Elon Musk and Stephen Miller.

Fandom Pulse also pulled the numbers. None of the first 10 episodes made Nielsen’s weekly streaming top 10, and by June the show had an 85% critics score on Rotten Tomatoes next to a 52% audience score.

Kneon has loved Star Trek: The Next Generation since he was about 10, and he says the show just wasn’t good. He calls it “a CW show in space.” Even Enterprise star Dominic Keating said on his own podcast, with Picardo sitting across from him, that it was “a bit CW in space.”

Is Taika Waititi’s Star Wars movie canceled?

On ice, in his words. Waititi told Inverse, while promoting Klara and the Sun, “we’re going to actually put it on ice and we’re working on a different thing altogether.” Kneon guesses Rian Johnson’s long-promised Star Wars trilogy is dead too.

The hosts also get into artist Frank Cho’s claim, made in a podcast interview at New York Comic Con, that he has been banned from Marvel for three years. “I pissed off Kathleen Kennedy and she demanded Marvel ban me,” Cho said. He says it started with joke Star Wars sketch covers he drew as convention commissions, and that Kennedy ended the whole Star Wars sketch cover program over them. Bleeding Cool, which reported the interview, couldn’t find new Marvel work from Cho after 2022.

The hosts expect a lot more stories like this now that Kennedy is gone from Lucasfilm. Somebody, they figure, will write the tell-all.

Modern Warfare 4’s campaign reviews are strong, and early buyers on Steam rated it about 93% positive as of Monday. The full game, Switch 2 version included, arrives Friday, Oct. 23.

CNN and CBS News keep separate bosses under Skydance, but David Ellison says there are “absolutely operational efficiencies” to chase on the way to $6 billion in savings.

CNN also signed a multiyear AI deal with Google that pays it for its journalism. Neither side shared the price.

Ecto Cooler is pouring again from the Freestyle machines at the World of Coca-Cola in Atlanta, minus the neon green.

Linda Fiorentino played Agent L at the end of Men in Black, then left movies after a small 2009 comedy and never said why.

Nintendo’s Power Glove started as a $10,000 virtual reality glove that its designers rebuilt out of about $26 worth of materials.

CHATGPT WASN’T JUST TRAINED TO PREDICT WORDS.

IT WAS ALSO TRAINED TO LEARN WHAT HUMANS PREFER.

That’s where RLHF comes in.

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback.

Here’s the idea:

Give an AI the same question.

It produces two different answers.

Humans compare them and choose which one is better.

Those preferences become training data.

Then:

1. HUMAN FEEDBACK
People rank competing AI responses.

2. REWARD MODEL
A model learns to predict which responses humans would prefer.

3. REINFORCEMENT LEARNING
The AI is optimized to produce responses that score better under that learned reward.

The result?

The model becomes better aligned with the preferences represented in its training feedback.

But there’s a catch.

The reward model is only a proxy for human judgment.

If it rewards the wrong things, the AI can learn to produce answers that score well without actually being better.

That’s why preference data, reward modeling, and evaluation all matter.

The big idea:

Pretraining teaches a model patterns in data.

RLHF helps shape how it responds.

AI alignment isn't just about making models smarter.

It's also about teaching them which responses humans prefer.
